title: Interference: what the interposed piece costs
outcomes: Counts the attackers and the defenders of the interposed piece before choosing an interference
Says whether the opponent can capture the interposed piece and so restore the cut line
Predicts how a missing defender or one extra attacker changes the verdict

steps.text:
This lesson follows **Interference: cut the line between two pieces**, which taught how to find the interposing move. Now put a price on it.
Before you interpose, ask: can the opponent simply capture the interposed piece? If they can, does the capture put a piece back on the cut line? A **defended** interposed piece can still be taken with gain when it is attacked more often than it is defended.

steps.caption: White to move. The pawn can step onto c7, between the black queen and the knight on f4. Nothing defends c7.

line.say: The pawn cuts the diagonal and attacks the queen.
The queen takes the pawn for nothing. From c7 it defends the knight again.

claims.statement: Nothing defends the pawn on c7.
Along the engine line the interference wins nothing.

steps.text:
**It holds** when the interposed piece cannot be taken with gain and the cut line was the target's only defence.
**It fails** when the piece is undefended, or attacked more often than defended, so the capturer lands back on the line.
**Rule of thumb:** count attackers and defenders of the interposed square first; an attacker of lower value than the interposed piece wins material even against a defender.

steps.title: Same interference, one change
steps.prompt: Same position and the same pawn move, one change each time. Predict, then check.
Before you interposed in the silent positions, what did you count: attackers of the interposed piece, its defenders, or only the line you wanted to cut? Which of the three did you skip?
